label: Sayings CLVIII–CLXXXIX
paragraphs: CLVIII. If you want to make progress, bear with being thought foolish and stupid where external things are concerned. Do not wish to be thought to know anything; and if some people think you are somebody, distrust yourself.

CLIX. Remember that you must behave as you would at a dinner party. Something is being passed round and comes to you: put out your hand and take a portion politely. It goes by: do not hold it back. It has not come yet: do not send your desire out ahead toward it, but wait until it comes to you. Do the same toward children, toward a wife, toward offices, toward wealth, and someday you will be worthy to dine with the gods. And if you do not even take what is set before you, but look past it, then you will not only dine with the gods but rule with them.

CLX. Remember that you are an actor in a play, of whatever kind the playwright chooses: short if he wants it short, long if he wants it long. If he wants you to play a beggar, see that you play even that part with skill; and the same if it is a lame man, a magistrate, a private citizen. For this is your business, to play well the role you are given; to choose it belongs to another.
CLXI. Let death and exile and everything that seems terrible be before your eyes every day, and death most of all; and you will never have a mean thought, and never desire anything too much.
CLXII. As a target is not set up to be missed, so nothing evil by nature comes to be in the universe.

CLXIII. As for piety toward the gods, know that the most important thing is this: to hold right opinions about them, that they exist and govern the whole well and justly, and to have set yourself to this, to obey them and to yield to everything that happens and to follow it willingly, as something brought about by the best of minds. For in that way you will never blame the gods, or accuse them of neglecting you.

CLXIV. Set down for yourself, now, a certain character and pattern, which you will keep both when you are by yourself and when you meet with people. And for the most part be silent, or say what is necessary and in few words. On rare occasions, when the moment calls for speech, speak; but not about any of the common topics: not about gladiators, not about horse races, not about athletes, not about food or drink, the things people talk about everywhere; and above all not about people, blaming or praising or comparing them. If you can, then, bring the conversation of your companions round by your own to what is fitting. But if you find yourself cut off among strangers, be silent.
CLXV. Do not laugh much, or at many things, or without restraint.
CLXVI. Refuse to take an oath, altogether if you can; if not, as far as circumstances allow.

CLXVII. Avoid dinners given by outsiders and laymen. But if the occasion ever arises, keep your attention on the stretch, so that you do not slip into the ways of laymen. For know that if a companion is dirty, the man who rubs up against him is bound to get dirty too, even if he happens to be clean himself.
CLXVIII. In what concerns the body, take only as much as bare need requires: food, drink, clothing, house, household slaves. Cut out everything that is for show or luxury.

CLXIX. If someone reports to you that so-and-so is speaking ill of you, do not defend yourself against what was said, but answer, "He must not have known my other faults, or he would not have mentioned only these."

CLXX. When you go to see one of the powerful, put it to yourself that you will not find him at home, that you will be shut out, that the doors will be slammed in your face, that he will take no notice of you. And if it is your duty to go even so, go and bear what happens, and never say to yourself, "It was not worth it." For that is a layman's way, the way of one at odds with external things.

CLXXI. In conversation, keep away from talking much and at length about your own deeds and dangers. For it is not as pleasant for others to hear what happened to you as it is for you to recall your dangers. Keep away from raising a laugh too; for it is a slippery habit that slides into the ways of laymen, and it is enough to loosen the respect your neighbors have for you. It is dangerous also to drift into foul talk. When anything of the kind happens, then, if the moment is right, rebuke the man who has gone that far; if not, make it plain by falling silent, and blushing, and frowning, that you dislike what is being said.

CLXXII. When you do something because you have decided it ought to be done, never avoid being seen doing it, even if most people are likely to think badly of it. For if you are not acting rightly, avoid the act itself; and if you are, why fear those who will be wrong to reproach you?

CLXXIII. It is a sign of a dull nature to spend much time on the things of the body: to exercise a great deal, eat a great deal, drink a great deal, spend a long time relieving yourself and making love. These things should be done in passing; let all your attention be turned to the mind.

CLXXIV. Everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, do not take hold of it by this handle, that he is wronging you, for that is the handle by which it cannot be carried; take it rather by the other, that he is your brother, that you were brought up together, and you will be taking hold of it where it can be carried.

CLXXV. Never call yourself a philosopher, and do not talk much among laymen about the teachings; do what follows from the teachings. At a dinner party, for instance, do not say how people ought to eat; eat as you ought. For remember that Socrates had so completely done away with display that people came to him wanting to be introduced to philosophers by him, and he took them along. So well did he bear being overlooked. And if talk about some teaching comes up among laymen, be silent for the most part; for there is great danger that you will at once vomit up what you have not digested. And when someone tells you that you know nothing, and it does not sting you, then know that you are beginning the work.

CLXXVI. When you have fitted yourself to live cheaply in what concerns the body, do not preen yourself on it; and if you drink water, do not say at every opportunity that you drink water. And if you ever want to train yourself for hardship, do it for yourself and not for outsiders. Do not hug statues.

CLXXVII. When someone gives himself airs because he can understand and explain the books of Chrysippus, say to yourself, "If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, this man would have nothing to give himself airs about. But what do I want? To understand nature and to follow it. So I look for someone to explain it; and hearing that Chrysippus does, I go to him. But I do not understand what he wrote; so I look for someone to explain that. And so far there is nothing to be proud of. When I have found the one who explains, what remains is to act on what I am told; that alone is something to be proud of. But if what I admire is the explaining itself, what have I turned out but a grammarian instead of a philosopher? Except that I explain Chrysippus instead of Homer. So when someone says to me, 'Read me some Chrysippus,' I blush instead, when I cannot show deeds that match the words and agree with them."
CLXXVIII. At your feasts, remember that you are entertaining two guests, body and soul; and whatever you give the body you have poured away at once, but whatever you give the soul you keep for good.
CLXXIX. At meals, take care that those who serve are not more than those who are served; for it is absurd that many souls should slave for a few couches.

CLXXX. It is best if, working with your own hands in the preparations and sitting down to the meal, you share what there is with those who serve. But if that is difficult at the time, remember that you, who are not tired, are being served by people who are tired; you are eating and they are not, drinking and they are not, talking and they are silent, at ease and they are under constraint. Then you will not flare up and do something out of place yourself, and you will not provoke another into doing something harsh.

CLXXXI. When Xanthippe was scolding Socrates for preparing so little for the friends he had invited, he said, "If they are our friends, they will not mind; and if they are not, we will not mind about them."
CLXXXII. Asked who the rich man is, Epictetus said, "The one who is content."

CLXXXIII. The same Epictetus, as I heard from Favorinus too, used to say that there are two faults far graver and uglier than all the rest, want of endurance and want of restraint: when we do not bear and put up with the wrongs that must be borne, or do not forbear from the things and the pleasures we ought to forbear from. "So," he said, "if a man takes these two words to heart, and sees to it that he commands himself by them and watches himself by them, he will for the most part be free from fault and will live a most peaceful life." The two words, he used to say, were anechou and apechou.

CLXXXIV. On every occasion we should have these ready at hand: "Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, to wherever you have long since assigned me. I will follow without flinching; and if I am unwilling and turn coward, I will follow all the same." "Whoever yields to necessity as he should, we count him wise, and he knows the things of the gods." "Well, Crito, if this is what pleases the gods, so be it." "Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot harm me."
CLXXXV. And we shall be followers of Socrates when we can write hymns of praise in prison.

CLXXXVI. It is hard to mix and bring together these two things, the care of a man who is attached to the materials and the steadiness of a man who pays them no attention; but it is not impossible. Otherwise happiness would be impossible. It is like what we do on a voyage. What can I do? Choose the helmsman, the sailors, the day, the moment. Then a storm falls on us. What does it matter to me now? My part has been done. The business belongs to another, the helmsman. But the ship is going down as well. What can I do, then? I do the only thing I can: I drown without fear, without screaming, without accusing God, knowing that what has been born must also perish. For I am not eternity, but a human being, a part of the whole as an hour is of the day. I must come like the hour, and like an hour pass.

CLXXXVII. And now we are sending you to Rome as a scout. But no one sends a coward as a scout, a man who, if he only hears a noise or sees a shadow somewhere, comes running back in a panic and says the enemy are already here. So now, if you come and tell us, "Things in Rome are frightening. Death is terrible, exile is terrible, abuse is terrible, poverty is terrible. Run, men, the enemy are here," we will say to you, "Go away and prophesy to yourself. Our only mistake was sending a scout like you." Diogenes, who was sent out as a scout before you, has brought us back a different report. He says that death is not an evil, for it is not shameful either. He says that ill repute is the noise of madmen. And what things this scout has said about pain, about pleasure, about poverty! He says that to be naked is better than any purple-bordered robe; he says that to sleep on the bare ground is the softest bed. And as proof of each he offers his own courage, his peace of mind, his freedom, and then his body too, glowing and hard. "No enemy is near," he says. "Everything is full of peace."

CLXXXVIII. If a man has this peace, proclaimed not by Caesar—for how could he proclaim it?—but by God through reason, is he not content when he is alone, when he looks and reflects: "Now no evil can happen to me. For me there is no robber, for me there is no earthquake; everything is full of peace, everything untroubled. Every road, every city, every gathering, neighbor, companion is harmless. Another provides my food, whose care it is; another my clothing; another gave me my senses, another my preconceptions. And when he does not provide what is needed, he is sounding the recall; he has opened the door and says to you, 'Come.' Where? To nothing terrible, but to where you came from, to what is friendly and akin to you, to the elements. What there was of fire in you will go back to fire; what there was of earth, to earth; of breath, to breath; of water, to water. There is no Hades, no Acheron, no Cocytus, no Pyriphlegethon; everything is full of gods and divine powers." A man who has these things to think about, and who sees the sun and the moon and the stars, and enjoys the earth and the sea, is no more lonely than he is helpless.

CLXXXIX. What, then, do you want to be doing when death finds you? For my part, I would want it to be some work that befits a human being, that does good, that serves the common benefit, that is noble. But if I cannot be found doing such great things, then at least this, which cannot be hindered, which is given to me: setting myself right, working on the power that uses impressions, laboring at freedom from passion, giving my relationships their due. If death overtakes me in the midst of these things, it is enough for me if I can lift up my hands to God and say, "The means I received from you for perceiving your governance and following it, I have not neglected. I have not disgraced you, so far as it lay with me. See how I have used my senses, see how I have used my preconceptions. Did I ever blame you? Was I ever discontented with anything that happened, or did I wish it otherwise? Did I break my relationships? That you brought me into being, I am grateful; I am grateful for what you gave. The time I have had the use of what is yours is enough for me. Take it back again and put it wherever you will. For it was all yours; you gave it to me." Is it not enough to go out in that state? What life is better or more becoming than that of a man in that state, and what end is happier?

divergences.lectio: "spend a long time relieving yourself and making love"
divergences.note: Epictetus names the two things Crossley folded into one polite phrase: emptying the bowels and coupling. The English is as plain as the register allows; the Greek verbs are blunter still (the second is the word for animals mating).

divergences.phrase: Verba haec duo dicebat: ἀνέχου et ἀπέχου
divergences.older: "He meant the words [Greek: Anechou kai apechou]—'Bear and Forbear.'" (Crossley; the brackets and the gloss are his)
divergences.lectio: "The two words, he used to say, were anechou and apechou."
divergences.note: The source is Latin: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights XVII.19, reporting Favorinus. Gellius gives the two Greek words and no translation, because he has just explained them (intolerantia, incontinentia). Lectio does the same: the Greek words are named once, transliterated without accents (Meditations policy 7), and the English "bear" and "forbear" are placed in Gellius's explanation, where his Latin has ferre and tenere. "I heard" is Gellius speaking; Crossley turned it into "Favorinus tells us".

divergences.lectio: Crossley's two sayings put into current English
divergences.note: Xanthippe and the dinner, and "Who is the rich man?", are fragments from the late anthologies in Schweighäuser's collection. Schenkl does not print them and no Greek was to hand (they are Schweighäuser's fragments 173 and 172); these two paragraphs are made from Crossley's English, checked against George Long's independent version (1877), and need the Greek before the edition is called ready. CLXXVIII–CLXXX, by contrast, are from the Stobaean maxims Schenkl does print (Gnomologium 20, 23, 24), read from the scan.
